title: Current-Voltage Relations and Ohmic/Non-Ohmic Resistance
topicTitle: Current-voltage relations; ohmic and non-ohmic resistance
notes: **Ohmic conductor:** obeys Ohm's law. The $I$-$V$ graph is a straight line through the origin. Resistance is constant.
**Non-ohmic conductor:** does not obey Ohm's law. The $I$-$V$ graph is curved. Resistance changes with voltage or current.

**Examples of non-ohmic:** diode (conducts easily in one direction only), filament lamp (resistance increases with temperature as current increases), thermistor (resistance decreases with temperature).
**Why filament lamp is non-ohmic:** as current increases, the filament heats up, increasing its resistivity. The $I$-$V$ curve bends because $R$ is not constant.
**Dynamic resistance:** $R_d = dV/dI$ at a point on the $I$-$V$ curve. For non-ohmic devices, this is the useful measure of resistance at a specific operating point.
**Forward bias diode:** current flows easily once the voltage exceeds the threshold ($\\\\approx 0.7$ V for silicon, $\\\\approx 0.3$ V for germanium). Below threshold, very little current flows.
**Reverse bias diode:** almost no current flows (except a tiny leakage current). At the breakdown voltage, current increases sharply and the diode may be damaged.
**Thermistor:** a semiconductor device whose resistance decreases sharply with temperature (NTC type). Used as temperature sensors and inrush current limiters.
**Zener diode:** operates in reverse breakdown at a precise voltage. It maintains a nearly constant voltage across it, used as a voltage regulator.

**Filament lamp $I$-$V$ curve:** starts linearly at low voltage (cool filament, low resistance). At higher voltages, the curve bends toward the voltage axis as the filament heats and resistance increases.

**Temperature coefficient of filament:** tungsten has $\\\\alpha \\\\approx 0.0045$ $^{\\\\circ}$C$^{-1}$. A 100 W, 230 V bulb has cold resistance of about $50\\\\,\\\\Omega$ but hot resistance of $529\\\\,\\\\Omega$.
confusion: Ohm's law $V = IR$ is a definition of resistance, not a law that all materials obey. Only ohmic conductors have a linear $I$-$V$ relationship. For non-ohmic devices, $R = V/I$ is still defined but varies.

A filament lamp becomes a better conductor (lower resistance) when cold. This is why bulbs often burn out at the moment they are switched on - the initial current surge is 10 times the steady-state current.

The dynamic resistance $dV/dI$ is different from the static resistance $V/I$. For a non-ohmic device, the static resistance is $V/I$ while the dynamic resistance is the slope of the $I$-$V$ curve at that point.

A diode is not simply a 'one-way valve' for current. In reverse bias, a tiny leakage current (nA to $\\\mu$A range) still flows. In forward bias, the current is exponentially related to voltage, not linearly.

Thermistors are not simply temperature-dependent resistors. Their resistance changes exponentially with temperature: $R = R_0 e^{\ eta(1/T - 1/T_0)}$, which makes them highly sensitive to small temperature changes.
practice: A filament lamp has a resistance of $20\\\\,\\\\Omega$ when cold and $240\\\\,\\\\Omega$ when glowing at full brightness. If connected to a 12 V supply, find the current when cold and when glowing. Solution: Cold: $I = V/R = 12/20 = 0.6$ A. Glowing: $I = V/R = 12/240 = 0.05$ A. The inrush current is 12 times the steady-state current.

A silicon diode has a forward voltage drop of 0.7 V at a current of 10 mA. It is connected in series with a 500 $\\\Omega$ resistor and a 5 V battery. Find the current. Solution: The diode drops 0.7 V, so the resistor sees $5 - 0.7 = 4.3$ V. $I = 4.3/500 = 8.6$ mA.

A thermistor has resistance $R_0 = 10\\\\,\	ext{k}\\\\Omega$ at 25$^{\\\\circ}$C and $R = 2\\\\,\	ext{k}\\\\Omega$ at 50$^{\\\\circ}$C. Find the resistance at 0$^{\\\\circ}$C assuming a linear temperature coefficient. Solution: $\\\\alpha = (R_0 - R)/(R \\\\cdot \\\\Delta T) = (10000 - 2000)/(2000 \	imes 25) = 0.16$ $^{\\\\circ}$C$^{-1}$. At 0$^{\\\\circ}$C: $R = R_0/(1 + \\\\alpha \\\\cdot 25) = 10000/(1 + 4) = 2000\\\\,\\\\Omega$.

A $I$-$V$ graph of a device shows that at $V = 3$ V, the current is 0.15 A, and the tangent at that point has slope $dI/dV = 0.02$ A/V. Find the static resistance and dynamic resistance. Solution: Static resistance $R_s = V/I = 3/0.15 = 20\\\\,\\\\Omega$. Dynamic resistance $R_d = 1/(dI/dV) = 1/0.02 = 50\\\\,\\\\Omega$.

A Zener diode with breakdown voltage 6 V is connected in parallel with a load resistor of 1 k$\\\Omega$ across a 10 V battery with series resistor of 500 $\\\Omega$. Find the current through the Zener diode. Solution: Voltage across load: 6 V (clamped by Zener). Current through 500 $\\\Omega$: $I = (10 - 6)/500 = 8$ mA. Current through load: $I_L = 6/1000 = 6$ mA. Current through Zener: $I_Z = 8 - 6 = 2$ mA.
universalFacts: A tungsten filament lamp has a resistance that changes by a factor of 10-15 between cold and hot, making it a classic example of non-ohmic behavior due to temperature-dependent resistivity.

The threshold voltage of a silicon diode is approximately 0.7 V because this is the energy needed to overcome the potential barrier of the p-n junction, corresponding to the band gap energy of silicon.
Semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance (NTC thermistors) because more charge carriers are thermally excited across the band gap, increasing conductivity.
Ohmic materials include most metals at constant temperature. Non-ohmic materials include all semiconductors, electrolytes, and any device where temperature or other conditions change with current.
The $I$-$V$ characteristic of a diode is exponential: $I = I_0(e^{eV/kT} - 1)$, where $I_0$ is the reverse saturation current, $k$ is Boltzmann's constant, and $T$ is temperature.
summary: An ohmic conductor obeys Ohm's law, so its I-V graph is a straight line through the origin and its resistance R = V/I stays constant at every operating point. A non-ohmic conductor does not: its I-V graph is curved because the resistance itself changes with the applied voltage or current, which is why R = V/I remains a valid definition of resistance while no longer being a constant of the material. Familiar non-ohmic devices include the diode, which conducts freely in only one direction once the forward voltage exceeds a threshold of about 0.7 V for silicon or 0.3 V for germanium, the filament lamp, whose resistance rises as the filament heats with increasing current, and the thermistor, whose resistance falls as it heats. For such devices the useful measure of resistance at a chosen operating point is the dynamic or differential resistance R_d = dV/dI, the slope of the I-V curve, which differs from the static resistance V/I.
importantConcepts: Ohmic conductor: obeys Ohm's law, gives a straight-line I-V graph through the origin, and has constant resistance.
Non-ohmic conductor: curved I-V graph with a resistance that varies with voltage or current, though R = V/I is still a valid definition.
Filament lamp as the classic non-ohmic case, because the heating of the filament raises its resistivity as the current grows.
Thermistor, whose resistance decreases with temperature, giving the opposite curvature to a lamp.
Diode behaviour with a forward threshold of about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium, and negligible reverse current until breakdown.
Dynamic or differential resistance R_d = dV/dI as the slope of the I-V curve at a point, distinguished from the static resistance V/I.
importantStatements: An ohmic conductor has a linear I-V characteristic passing through the origin, so its resistance is independent of voltage and current.
For a non-ohmic conductor the ratio V/I changes with the operating point, so the resistance is not a fixed property of the device.
A filament lamp is non-ohmic because the filament's temperature, and therefore its resistivity, rises as the current increases.
A diode carries almost no current in reverse bias until the reverse voltage reaches breakdown, when the current rises sharply.
The dynamic resistance R_d = dV/dI of a non-ohmic device is the slope of its I-V curve at the point of interest.
importantTasks: Sketch the I-V graph of an ohmic and a non-ohmic conductor and label the differences between them.
Calculate the cold and operating resistance of a filament lamp and explain the large inrush current at switch-on.
Solve a circuit containing a diode in series with a resistor by allowing for the forward voltage drop of the diode.
Determine the dynamic resistance of a non-ohmic device from the slope of its I-V graph at a stated point.
keyPoints: Ohm's law V = IR is a definition of resistance, not a law obeyed by every material.
A cold filament has a much lower resistance than a glowing one, which is why bulbs often fail at the instant of switch-on.
The inrush current through a cold bulb can be about ten times the steady-state current.
Use V/I for the static resistance and the tangent slope dV/dI for the dynamic resistance of a non-ohmic device.
A diode in series with a resistor reduces the voltage available to the resistor by the diode's forward drop.
specialNotes: R = V/I is always a valid definition of resistance, but it is only a constant, and hence a material property, for an ohmic conductor.
A filament lamp is a better conductor when cold, so the initial current surge at switch-on is far larger than the steady current and can burn the filament.
Below the forward threshold a silicon diode passes essentially no current, so a diode is close to an open circuit in that region and near a short circuit once forward biased.
The static resistance V/I and the dynamic resistance dV/dI are different quantities and coincide only for a straight-line characteristic.
A non-ohmic device has no single resistance at all, so a stated operating point or temperature must always accompany the value quoted.
examShortTricks: Check the graph shape first: a straight line through the origin means ohmic and any curvature means non-ohmic, which alone settles a descriptive question.
For a diode, subtract the forward drop before doing Ohm's law on the series resistor, so the resistor sees V_supply − 0.7 V for silicon.
Quote the cold and hot resistances of a lamp separately; at fixed voltage the ratio of the two currents equals the ratio of the two resistances.
Remember 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium, and treat a reverse-biased diode as an open circuit unless breakdown is specified.
examNotes: A three mark question commonly gives the cold and glowing resistance of a lamp and asks for the current in each case from a fixed supply.
Sketching and labelling I-V graphs for ohmic and non-ohmic conductors is a very common two or three mark item.
Numericals on a diode plus resistor in series with a battery appear regularly and test the forward voltage drop.
One mark definition questions ask for an ohmic and a non-ohmic conductor, with the filament lamp and diode as standard examples.
practiceQuestions: A filament lamp has a resistance of 20 Ω when cold and 240 Ω when glowing. Find the current in each case from a 12 V supply.
Sketch the I-V characteristic of a metallic conductor and of a filament lamp, labelling both axes.
A silicon diode with a 0.7 V forward drop is in series with a 500 Ω resistor and a 5 V battery. Find the current.
Explain, using the temperature dependence of resistivity, why a filament lamp is non-ohmic.
Distinguish between the static resistance V/I and the dynamic resistance dV/dI for a non-ohmic conductor.
